title: A highly prevalent lupus risk haplotype increases IRF7-dependent induction of IFN-α, enhancing antiviral defense and exacerbating autoimmunity.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Read the full article text from PubMed Central (PMC13592154, 110k characters) including its data-availability paragraph and methods. Listed the GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus, a public repository of gene-activity data) record GSE312190 and its file directory: 24 RNA-seq samples, one 3.9 GB raw archive, 24 coverage tracks of 117-186 MB each, and per-sample Salmon transcript-abundance files (quant.sf.gz). Read one sample record (GSM9340148) to confirm the processed file type. Probed every route to the six supplementary files (one PDF, five Excel workbooks) named in the article XML: Europe PMC refuses them with 'Article with id PMC13592154 is not open access one'; the PMC /bin/ path returns a 1.8 kB HTML challenge page instead of the file; the PMC open-access package service returns 404 on both hosts.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the protein-binding microarray (PBM, a glass slide carrying thousands of short DNA sequences that measures how strongly a protein sticks to each one): the 10,410 synthetic interferon-stimulated response element probes (6,954 with a 2-base spacer, 3,456 with a 3-base spacer), built from 76 plus 36 seed sites and all their single-letter variants, and the per-probe median fluorescence values for the risk and protective IRF7 versions. I never saw that table. Also text-only: the lupus genome-wide association analysis in European and African ancestry cohorts, the ancient-DNA frequency bins, and all mouse and cell-culture assay numbers.

a1_downloadable.note: The only table big enough for machine learning — the 10,410-probe DNA-binding measurements — is deposited nowhere. The paper says 'all other data are included in the article and supplemental information', and the supplement itself is not retrievable: Europe PMC returns 'not open access', the PMC /bin/ path returns an HTML challenge page, the open-access package service 404s. Only the 24-sample RNA-seq in GEO GSE312190 actually downloads.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: No label column exists in anything downloadable. The per-probe binding strength I would predict would have to be lifted out of figure panels or an Excel workbook I cannot open, and the RNA-seq gives only gene-level fold changes between three cell lines.

a3_inputs_present.note: The DNA probe sequences are not in this paper at all; the array design is cited to Andrilenas et al. 2018 (Nucleic Acids Research), so the model inputs would have to be reconstructed from a different paper's supplement.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are stated in the text: median probe fluorescence normalised by MicroArray LINEar Regression for the binding assay, counts-per-million for the RNA coverage tracks. Stated in the paper, not seen in a file.

a5_enough_rows.note: What is actually downloadable is 24 RNA-seq samples (three THP-1 monocyte lines and two HEK lines, in triplicate, with and without stimulation). That is 24 rows at the unit of analysis, far under the ~1,500 needed. The 10,410 probe rows exist only in the inaccessible supplement, and they cover just two protein variants.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~30 MB of Salmon transcript-abundance files for 24 samples; the 3.9 GB raw archive and 24 coverage tracks (117-186 MB each) would be skipped
a6_fits_laptop.note: File sizes read from the GEO FTP directory listing. The usable part is tiny; size is not the problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: GEO's 24 samples match the design described in the paper (3 THP-1 lines x 2 conditions x 3 replicates, plus 2 HEK lines x 3 replicates). I could not cross-check the 10,410 probe count against any file.

a8_label_provenance.note: Provenance is clean where it exists: binding strength is a direct fluorescence measurement and expression is sequencing-based, so neither is another model's output. This passes on paper description only — it is moot given A1.

existing_models.name: DeepBind (2015 convolutional neural network for DNA- and RNA-binding protein sequence preferences)
existing_models.score_and_split: Trained and evaluated on protein-binding microarray and chromatin-immunoprecipitation data; the original paper reports held-out-probe accuracy per experiment. I retrieved the Nature Biotechnology record but did not extract a specific number for an interferon-regulatory-factor array.

existing_models.name: DeepPBS (2024 geometric deep-learning model predicting protein-DNA binding preference from structure, Nature Methods)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported to work across protein families on both experimental and predicted protein-DNA structures; specific numbers not extracted.

existing_models.name: FamilyCode (2024-2025 biophysically interpretable model predicting how a missense change in a transcription factor shifts its DNA letter preferences, Nucleic Acids Research)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported R-squared 0.94 (root-mean-square deviation 0.37) for ASCL2 mutants and R-squared 0.98 at one motif position, validated against SELEX-seq binding models.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The authors frame the open problem as the sheer number of natural human transcription-factor variants being too large to test experimentally.

backbone.name: DNABERT-2 or HyenaDNA (DNA language models) would fit a sequence-to-binding task, and ESM-2 (a protein language model) the protein side
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU would suffice for ~10,000 short DNA probes, if the probes existed in a file
backbone.licence: Backbone licences are permissive; irrelevant because the training data is unavailable

integration.partner_dataset: CIS-BP build 2.00 and the UniPROBE/JASPAR motif collections, joinable if the probe sequences and intensities were ever released
integration.join_key: DNA sequence string / transcription-factor gene symbol
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does a single common coding change in a human immune transcription factor shift its DNA letter preferences enough that a sequence model trained on reference-genome motifs mispredicts which promoters it turns on? — a good question that this paper's released data cannot answer.

controls.positive_control: Would have been reproducing the reported Pearson correlation of 0.95 between this study's risk-haplotype probe intensities and the 2018 purified IRF7 dimer intensities. Not runnable without the probe table.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling across probes; not runnable.
controls.external_validation: Andrilenas et al. 2018 Nucleic Acids Research binding data for IRF3, IRF5 and IRF7 dimers would be a genuine second source, but it belongs to a different paper.

honest_claim_h3: No honest claim is available from the downloadable data: with 24 RNA-seq samples across five cell lines, any model would be describing three cell lines rather than predicting anything transferable.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a short DNA sequence to predict how strongly two versions of the immune protein IRF7 bind to it.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example would be one synthetic DNA probe (an interferon-stimulated response element variant) plus which IRF7 version was tested; the paper describes 10,410 such probes, but I verified no file containing them.
plain_idea.predict: The measured stickiness of IRF7 to that probe — median fluorescence from a nuclear-extract protein-binding microarray, a glass slide where a tagged protein is washed over thousands of DNA spots and the glow is photographed.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Lupus geneticists and transcription-factor modellers would learn whether a common coding variant carried by much of the world's population measurably rewires which gene promoters get switched on, which no reference-genome-trained model currently accounts for.

ml_idea: Predict nuclear-extract protein-binding-microarray fluorescence from the DNA probe sequence, separately for the lupus-risk and protective IRF7 haplotypes, and ask whether the allele-specific difference in binding is itself predictable from sequence; held out by seed site so the model must generalise to unseen interferon-stimulated response elements. Dead on arrival because the probe sequences and intensities are in no repository and in a supplement that cannot be downloaded.

effort.compute_note: Only the 24 Salmon transcript-abundance files are reachable, roughly 30 MB total, so compute is trivial and irrelevant. All figures are estimates from the GEO file listing; nothing was timed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Try to download the supplementary Excel workbooks. I did: Europe PMC rejects the article as not open access, the PMC /bin/ path serves a challenge page, and the open-access package service 404s. That one check kills it in five minutes.

verdict_reason: Fails A1, A2, A3 and A5. The only machine-learning-sized table in the paper — 10,410 DNA probes with IRF7 binding strength for the risk and protective haplotypes — is deposited in no repository and sits in supplementary Excel files that cannot be retrieved by any route (Europe PMC calls the article not open access; PMC's file path returns a challenge page). What does download is GEO GSE312190: 24 RNA-seq samples from five cell lines, which is 24 rows at the unit of analysis. The probe sequences themselves are not even in this paper, being cited to Andrilenas et al. 2018. This is an excellent mechanistic genetics paper and a poor machine-learning candidate; if the authors ever deposit the binding microarray table, the allele-specific sequence-to-binding task would be worth re-opening.
